To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the prevalence of polygyny declined by 60% in Zimbabwe between 1998 and 2011, 2) polygyny accounted for only 25% of concurrency, and 3) polygyny was not a stable form of concurrency.

(1) multiple partnerships, non-marital concurrency and polygyny all declined in prevalence by around 60-70%, (2) polygyny accounted for 25% of concurrency, (3) polygynous husbands were more likely to divorce or separate from their wives, and (4) polygynously married men reported more casual sex partners.

(1) the proportion of men reporting multiple partnerships, non-marital concurrency and polygyny decreased by 60% to 70%, (2) polygyny is not a stable form of concurrency and (3) polygynous relationships do not protect men from subsequent divorce/separation or casual sex partnerships.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of polygyny in the decline of HIV in Zimbabwe.
understanding the role of multiple partnerships, non-marital concurrency and polygyny on the HIV epidemic in eastern Zimbabwe.
trends in sexual partnerships during a period of decline in the prevalence of HIV infection in Zimbabwe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all partnership types were equally important to HIV decline in Zimbabwe.
all forms of multiple partnership, including polygyny, contributed to the HIV decline in Zimbabwe.
multiple partnerships, nonmonogamy, and polygamy all declined in this population during the observed period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decline in partnerships is likely to have been a major contributor to the decline in HIV prevalence.
the declines in partnerships were not due to a reduction in polygyny, but that polygyny was not an effective way to reduce partnerships.

multiple partnerships are a key factor in HIV epidemics and that polygyny should be considered a form of concurrency, but it is a less important driver of HIV transmission than nonmarital concurrency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the epidemiological impact of polygyny is likely to be small, but that the impact of other forms of multiple partnerships is likely to be substantial.
multiple partnerships and concurrency declined substantially during a period of HIV prevalence declines.
multiple partnerships and concurrency are not the same, and the former may not be as important to population-level HIV declines as the latter.
